prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength concept and its realisation at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a two-laureate prize and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. The part of the lattice clock that the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not cover is specific. The comb made optical frequencies countable, and the 2012 work controlled and probed single ions. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a different idea: it cancels the lattice light shift to first order while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel, which trades the single-ion route's weak signal for a large gain in stability. Ye's group then showed that this route reaches a systematic uncertainty at the 10^-18 level, with the stability to evaluate it in practice. The result has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in several countries, and it carries concrete uses in tests of constants and relativity, geodesy and the work towards redefining the second. The credit is clean and needs no forced name.
statement.case_against: The honest reservations stand. The lattice clock is a step within a recognised line, with comb and ion-control prizes behind it, and a committee that weights breadth of new physics could reasonably place B017 first. Other lattice-clock groups at SYRTE, PTB, NIST and RIKEN, and the priority sequence among record uncertainties, are not carried by two names. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so some of the payoff is still prospective, and tests of constant variation and dark matter have so far found nothing. The B017 case is stronger than the clock on breadth, but its attribution (Cao and other groups) and its still-debated superconducting mechanism are harder to repair in a citation than the clock's overlap is.

responses.point: Asks whether the lattice clock is only an incremental step in a recognised line and ranks it seventh because B017 opened a new field.
responses.response: The chair's question on distinctness deserves a specific answer, and mine is parallel many-atom interrogation at magic wavelength with the light shift cancelled. That is a different physical route from the ion clocks of 2012 and does not follow from the comb. I accept your breadth criterion and I would give it real weight, but I do not think it settles the ordering. A discovery prize also needs credit that survives scrutiny, and B017 still leaves out Yuan Cao and several parallel groups, which no citation fixes. I have not moved B017 above B015, but I keep it as my first alternative and I think reversing the order is a defensible judgement.

responses.point: Moved B017 to first place after finding no support for the condensate choice, and asks that the citation stay on the prediction and the observed correlated states.
responses.response: I share your preference for a B017 citation that names the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated insulating and superconducting states and does not claim the pairing mechanism. That wording does answer most of the maturity objection raised by Johansson-Goran and Pearce-Mark. It does not answer the credit boundary, because the Cao omission and the parallel work remain outside the names. Your own argument that five members placing it in their top three is better evidence of breadth than one enthusiast's choice is fair, and it is part of why I list B017 first among alternatives. I would still accept the weaker maturity argument here and rely on the credit boundary, which for B015 is cleaner.

responses.point: Agrees on the two-name B015 credit, records the overlap with other lattice-clock groups, and says an experimentalist trio for B016 would leave Zoller, Cirac and Jaksch out.
responses.response: I accept your point on B016. Allocating five names to three places is the reason I keep it only as a second alternative, and an experimentalist trio does leave out the theoretical origin, which I find as hard to defend as you do. I withdraw any suggestion that Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger alone would be a clean cut. On B015 we agree that the other groups are not covered. I would carry that in the citation by naming the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its 10^-18 realisation and not general frequency metrology, and I would not add a third name to meet it.

responses.point: Supports B015 but notes that its first-place support comes only from atomic and precision-measurement specialists, while B017 has broader top-three support.
responses.response: Your point about correlated enthusiasm applies to me as well, since I work in atomic theory and the clock is next to my field. I have therefore tried to rest my case on the physics, with the distinct many-atom magic-wavelength route and the reproduction by several groups, and not on the count of first places. Broader top-three support for B017 is real evidence, but it is also a count, and I would not let it decide. I would be more concerned about the pending redefinition of the second than you are: I read it as a consequence of the clock's maturity, not as a reason to wait for it.

responses.point: Argues that B051 is the most mature candidate, with two decades of confirmation, and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B051 is a settled discovery and that its scientific reality is not in doubt. My difficulty is with the credit and with the 2016 prize on topological phases, since the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, the Mele versus Hasan choice and the three-person cap leave the attribution less clean than for the clock, and the committee has fewer members behind it. I also read the chair's question on the 2016 prize as a real constraint on a second topology prize so soon. I keep B051 outside my alternatives, but the maturity case you make is the strongest on the list.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts many-atom magic-wavelength parallelism as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is the crux for B015.
Whether breadth of new physics should outrank a clean invention, in which case B017 would reasonably come first.
Whether the omission of other lattice-clock groups can be defended with two names, and whether the priority record is as clean as I recall; I have not verified it independently.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second is better read as a reason to act or to wait.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my profile documents a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and papers with the Lund attosecond group, collaborations with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and work with Reinhold Schuch, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero or the B016 names. B015 is neighbouring AMO and precision-measurement work, not my own subfield, and I leave the question of any recusal to the chair and the committee. I raised this in round 1 and no member has asked for a recusal.
